items.author: priya.n
items.title: Real-time defect detection on low-power ARM boards
items.body: Goal: run the defect detector at under 50 ms per frame on the Cortex-A72 inspection board (4 cores, no NPU) without losing more than 1 point of mAP. Current model: 92.4 mAP at 180 ms per frame. Customers on older lines cannot add a GPU box. We do not know whether a detector this small can keep accuracy on defects under 8 px once quantized; published INT8 results are mostly on ImageNet classification, not small-object detection.

items.author: omar.k
items.title: Baseline latency and accuracy on ARM board
items.body: Profile the FP32 detector on the Cortex-A72 board with the 1,240-image held-out set. Record per-layer latency and mAP by defect size bucket.

items.author: omar.k
items.body: Baseline done. FP32: 180 ms per frame, 92.4 mAP overall, 81.0 mAP on defects under 8 px. 61% of time is in the first three conv blocks. Full profile in the A1 experiment log.

items.author: li.w
items.title: Experiment 1: post-training INT8 quantization
items.body: Hypothesis: post-training static INT8 quantization with 500 calibration images gets us under 50 ms with under 1 point mAP loss, as reported for classification models.

items.author: li.w
items.body: Result: latency 41 ms (meets target) but mAP fell to 84.1 overall and to 58.3 on defects under 8 px. Hypothesis rejected. Small defects are lost because activation ranges in the first blocks are dominated by bright background pixels.

items.author: priya.n
items.body: Agree we close this as failed. Per-tensor calibration cannot represent the small-defect activations. Next: try pruning to keep FP32 precision, in parallel with a QAT plan.

items.author: omar.k
items.title: Experiment 2: structured channel pruning
items.body: Hypothesis: removing 50% of channels in the backbone keeps small-defect accuracy because precision stays FP32, and halves latency.

items.author: omar.k
items.body: Result: 50% pruning plus 20 epochs fine-tuning gives 88 ms and 90.9 mAP. Accuracy is fine but latency is not close to 50 ms. 70% pruning reaches 61 ms but mAP drops to 86.2. Closing as failed for the latency target.

items.author: li.w
items.title: Experiment 3: quantization-aware training with distillation
items.body: Hypothesis: quantization-aware training with per-channel weight scales, keeping the first and last layers in FP16, and distilling from the FP32 teacher recovers small-defect accuracy at INT8 speed.

items.author: li.w
items.body: Run 4 of 6: 46 ms per frame, 91.8 mAP overall, 79.6 mAP on defects under 8 px. Within 1 point of baseline overall. Mixed precision on the first block costs 5 ms versus full INT8.

items.author: priya.n
items.body: Repeated run 4 with three seeds: 91.6 to 91.9 mAP, 45 to 47 ms. Result is stable. Distillation weight 0.7 was the key setting; without distillation QAT gave 89.0 mAP.

items.author: omar.k
items.title: Thermal throttling check under continuous load
items.body: Run the QAT model for 8 hours on the line simulator. Check whether latency stays under 50 ms once the board heats up.

items.author: omar.k
items.body: After 2 hours the board throttles and latency rises to 58 ms. With the heatsink revision and 3 worker threads instead of 4, latency holds at 48 ms over 8 hours.

items.author: mei.c
items.title: Defect detection on reflective metal with under 200 labelled images
items.body: A new customer machines chrome and brushed aluminium parts. Specular highlights look like scratches to the current model. They can only provide 180 labelled images. Uncertainty: whether few-shot methods that work on matte surfaces transfer to specular surfaces at all. Target: recall 0.90 at a false-positive rate under 10%.

items.author: mei.c
items.title: Experiment 1: fine-tune existing detector on 180 images
items.body: Hypothesis: standard fine-tuning with heavy augmentation is enough for 180 images.

items.author: mei.c
items.body: Result: recall 0.62, false-positive rate 31%. Most false positives sit on specular highlights. Fine-tuning alone does not work.

items.author: mei.c
items.title: Experiment 2: synthetic specular highlight augmentation
items.body: Hypothesis: rendering synthetic highlights onto defect-free images teaches the model that highlights are not defects. Generate 2,000 augmented images with a Phong highlight model.

items.author: mei.c
items.body: Result: false-positive rate down to 18%, recall 0.66. Better but highlights with sharp edges still trigger detections. Synthetic highlights look too smooth.

items.author: priya.n
items.body: Worth testing a highlight mask as a preprocessing step instead of hoping the model learns it.

items.author: mei.c
items.title: Experiment 3: prototypical network with highlight masking
items.body: Hypothesis: masking saturated pixels before feature extraction, plus a prototypical few-shot head pretrained on our matte-surface data, separates highlights from scratches.

items.author: mei.c
items.body: Result: recall 0.81, false-positive rate 9%. Ablation: highlight masking alone gives most of the gain (FPR 31% to 14%), the prototypical head adds the rest. Recall is still below the 0.90 target.

items.author: li.w
items.body: Tried the A1 QAT recipe on this model: 52 ms on the ARM board, recall drops to 0.78. Specular model is harder to quantize.
